mostly unaffected by our modelling results. Testing 
these results based on independent survey data 
showed high odds that impairments and ultimately 
unpleasant places estimated by models match with 
those identified in the survey. Particularly, for the 
olfactory model we could find statistical evidence 
(p-value = 0.019) that modelled olfactory impair -
ments occur in the same areas as identified in the 
survey.
The modelling results for acoustic, olfactory and 
visual impairments show varying spatial patterns, 
thereby reemphasizing the importance to include 
multiple sensory aspects in aesthetic quality assess -
ment (Porteous 1982 ). Visual impairments can be 
found in 91% of the total area, whereas acoustic 
impairments impact 84% and olfactory impairments 
54%. Yet, looking at the impairment intensities, the 
highest categories (high and very high intensity) 
cover the largest area for acoustic impairments (30% 
of the study area) followed by visual (18%) and olfac -
tory (2%). Taking the specific example of a road, it 
means that even when the road is not well visible 
anymore the noise can still be heavily perceptible. 
Jeon and Jo ( 2020 ) show that there is a strong inter -
action of audio and visual information and that in 
combination they best performed to explain sounds -
cape and landscape components, such as pleasantness 
or naturalness.
In this study we have shown that all three impair -
ment types overlap in the immediate surroundings of 
the large river Lahn which dominates and characterizes 
the landscape. This calls for attention, as blue spaces 
have shown to be positively associated to mental health 
(Gascon et al. 2017 ) and to lead to higher momentary 
subjective wellbeing than urban fabric or indoor envir -
onments (MacKerron and Mourato 2013 ).
This apparent contradiction could be explained by the 
presence of a four-lane road right next at the southern 
shore following the river path. The finding highlights the 
importance to consider impairments in the analysis of 
aesthetic quality of the landscape. While approaches that 
not consider impairments and focus on positive aesthetic 
factors might have led to misleading high values for 
aesthetic quality of the landscape, the inclusion of impair -
ments in general and sensory impairments in particular 
allows researchers and planners to see the nearby road as 
well, especially if acoustic and olfactory impacts are 
strong as well.
6. Conclusions
The modelling applied here can be useful for land -
scape planning practice. By using hard-GIS approach 
to model impairments, indications of potentially 
unpleasant places can be generated. This information 
can form the basis for more in-depth, and eventually 
more focused, survey-based investigations of actual 
perceived unpleasant places. In addition, the informa -
tion can provide planners important information on 
where interventions are needed if the perceived qual -
ity of places for citizens should be enhanced. The 
results show by what types of impairments and in 
which intensity an area is affected by acoustic, visual 
and olfactory impairments. This information is not 
directly evident from assessments of the aesthetic 
quality of landscapes commonly found in landscape 
planning. Planners can use this information, supple -
mented by spatial assessment of the demand for areas 
suitable for recreation, to develop targeted measures 
aimed at reducing impairments and thereby increas -
ing recreation opportunities (Albert et al. 2019 ). 
Potential measures can then focus on minimizing 
the sources of impacts (for example suggestions to 
lower speed limits on roads to reduce acoustic 
impacts) or on amending existing impacts, for exam -
ple by planning wide-enough tree corridors along 
roads to reduce noise propagation. Further research 
may focus on testing the modelling approach in other 
regions, and by testing it together with planners, 
stakeholders and decision-makers in practice.
Hard- and soft-GIS methods can be seen as com -
plementary approaches. As demonstrated in this 
study, soft-GIS methods can be used to verify and 
complement hard-GIS methods, but also hard-GIS 
methods can provide basic information for subse -
quent in-depth survey-based investigations of actual 
perceived unpleasant places as discussed above. 
Results have shown that not only experiences asso -
ciated to sensory dimensions led participants to 
locate an unpleasant place.

study, soft-GIS methods can be used to verify and

methods can provide basic information for subse -
quent in-depth survey-based investigations of actual 
perceived unpleasant places as discussed above. 
Results have shown that not only experiences asso -
ciated to sensory dimensions led participants to 
locate an unpleasant place. Personal emotional 
experiences, such as sense of belonging or undesir -
able incidences, a lack of accessibility and safety, and 
social experiences, such as feeling bothered by other 
people, contributed as well to perceived unpleasant 
places. This is in line with previous studies, which 
found that various factors, such as noise, scariness, 
restricted access or unattractiveness, contributed to 
perceived place dissatisfaction (Tyrväinen et al. 2007 ; 
Kyttä et al. 2013 ; Raymond et al. 2016 ).
Combining hard-GIS methods with soft-GIS 
methods brings together ‘hard’ objective, register- 
based geodata with ‘soft’, subjective, experiential sur -
vey data and contributes to credibility, relevance and 
legitimacy of scientific findings for planning pro -
cesses and decision-making (Kyttä 2011 ; Durham 
et al. 2014 ). Therefore, utilizing both hard-GIS and 
soft-GIS methods and exploiting their complemen -
tary features helps to build a bridge between research 
and practice, between various professionals in the 
planning process, and between planning practices 
and inhabitants’ unique experiences of everyday life 
(Kahila and Kyttä 2009 ).

__data__.text:
Riesch 2011 ; Brown and Fagerholm 2015 ; Burkhard 
and Maes 2017 ). When assessing the impairments in 
the case study area, the land use data was connected 
to selected literature data. The distance values we 
used are conservative estimates commonly used in 
landscape planning in Germany. We argue that 
these conservative estimates are adequate for the 
field of application outlined above. They could be 
refined using more advanced modelling and using 
additional data. The biggest improvement might be 
gained from incorporating visibility analyses based on 
a digital surface model (relief and height of buildings 
and vegetation) to determine the areas actually 
impacted by visual impairments (compare e.g. 
Hernández et al. 2004 ). But the propagation of noise 
and smells could be modeled more accurately, too. 
This should lead to a more realistic representation of 
the on-site situation and to stronger correlations 
between modeled impairments and surveyed unplea -
sant places. These improvements, however, require 
more advanced modelling, more data, and empirical 
foundations, which are not always as readily available 
as land use data and conservative estimates. Hence, 
each step towards a more realistic representation of 
the actual on-site situation is a step towards less 
practicability, and time and cost efficiency for assess -
ments on broader scales. We would suggest incorpor -
ating such advanced modeling, complemented by on- 
site surveys, when planning and allocating measures 
as outlined above for areas preselected based on our 
results.
With regards to the comparison between the mod -
elling results and the survey data, a few issues can be 
noted. To evaluate the aesthetic quality model, the 
survey data on PPUE had to be categorized in the 
three impairment types, leading to three potential 
shortcomings. First, the PPUE survey question was 
not design to be categorized into impairment types, 
and thus the choice of statements, which was unequally 
distributed between the types may have influenced the 
results. Second, the breadth of PPUE had been reduced 
offering less detail on what exactly the perceived 
impairment of that place was. Third, some of the 
PPUEs did not fit into the categories provided by the 
aesthetic quality model (see Appendix 5). This did not 
only reduce the number of points, but also misses 
another dimension of aesthetic quality. Kyttä et al. 
( 2013 ) have shown that negatively perceived places 
are strongly related with factors describing social life, 
such as insecurity or bad reputation. Integrating more 
cognitive aspects indeed could further enhance the 
technocratic and expert based approach of landscape 
assessment (Dakin 2003 ).

Trace metal concentrations along tributary streams of historically mined
areas, Lower Lahn and Dill River basins, central Germany
Charles W. Martin
Department of Geography, 1002 Seaton Hall, Kansas State University, Manhattan, Kansas 66506-2904, USA
ARTICLE INFO
Keywords:
Trace metals
Floodplain metal storage
Mined watersheds
Sediment contamination
Germany
ABSTRACT
Watersheds with a history of mining frequently have high concentrations of trace metals stored in downstream
ﬂoodplain sediments. To assess the contribution of tributary streams to the elevated trace metal concentrations
previously documented along the lower Dill and lower Lahn Rivers of central Germany, I examined the con-
centrations of Cu, Pb, and Zn in fourteen cores collected from near-channel sediments along 9 tributary streams.
Five tributaries empty into the lower Dill River and 4 drain into the lower Lahn River. The tributary streams
drain areas that were mined for Fe, Cu, and Pb for more than a century, with the last mine closing in 1983. Cores
were also collected from near-channel sediments at 7 sites along the lower Lahn River to more broadly assess the
storage of trace metals along the river. Large quantities of Cu, Pb, and Zn from mining activity are not stored in
near-channel positions along the length of the sampled tributaries. Mean and median concentrations of Cu, Pb,
and Zn along the tributaries are less than the mean and median concentrations along the lower Dill and Lahn
Rivers; concentrations along the tributaries diﬀer little from background trace metal levels and are less than
contamination standards contained in the German Federal Soil Protection Act. The mean concentrations of Cu,
Pb, and Zn along the lower Lahn River are greater than background concentrations and mean concentrations
exceed contamination standards from the German Federal Soil Protection Act. Tributary streams are not a source
for the elevated trace metal concentrations found along the lower Dill and Lahn Rivers and mined areas will
likely not serve as a source of future heavy metal pollution. The results of this study indicate that the mining
process did not release large quantities of metals to theﬂuvial system.
1. Introduction
Contamination of ﬂoodplain soils and alluvium with trace metals
poses a long-term threat to the environment, especially when metals are
stored in geomorphically sensitive positions such as channel banks and
near-channel ﬂoodplains. Should the metals be remobilized during
ﬂoods or channel shifting, metal-contaminated sediments can be con-
veyed downstream. Trace metals typically originate from anthro-
pogenic activities such as industry, agriculture, and mining. In parts of
western Europe, trace metals have been discharged to the natural en-
vironment for many centuries (Matschullat et al., 1997;Brännvall et al.,
1999; Renberg et al., 2001). The peak discharge of metals to the en-
vironment is usually attributed to the period from the early- to mid-
nineteenth century until the early 1970s ( Renberg et al., 2001;
Middelkoop, 2002; De Vleeschouwer et al., 2007 ; Ciszewski and
Grygar, 2016; Dhivert et al., 2016). Mining activities have long been a
potential source of trace metals to theﬂuvial system. In Europe, trace
metal mining began as early as 3000 years ago (Monna et al., 2000),
and numerous studies have chronicled mining dating back centuries
throughout western Europe (e.g., Hudson-Edwards et al., 1999;
Mascaro et al., 2001;Coulthard and Macklin, 2003; Dennis et al., 2009;
Hürkamp et al., 2009; Foulds et al., 2014; Resongles et al., 2014;Beane
et al., 2016;Bird, 2016; Schillereﬀ et al., 2016;Horák and Hejeman,
2016). The vast majority of the mines have been closed for many years,
but contaminated sediments remain stored in channel banks and near-
channel sediments.

In Europe, trace
metal mining began as early as 3000 years ago (Monna et al., 2000),
and numerous studies have chronicled mining dating back centuries
throughout western Europe (e.g., Hudson-Edwards et al., 1999;
Mascaro et al., 2001;Coulthard and Macklin, 2003; Dennis et al., 2009;
Hürkamp et al., 2009; Foulds et al., 2014; Resongles et al., 2014;Beane
et al., 2016;Bird, 2016; Schillereﬀ et al., 2016;Horák and Hejeman,
2016). The vast majority of the mines have been closed for many years,
but contaminated sediments remain stored in channel banks and near-
channel sediments. In these geomorphically active zones, contaminated
sediments may be remobilized and carried downstream (James, 1989;
Marcus, 1989; Leigh, 1997; Förstner, 2003; Foulds et al., 2014; Lecce
and Pavlowsky, 2014;Clement et al., 2017).
In Europe, the impact of historical mining activity on rivers and
streams has been extensively documented. Studies from the UK have
shown that historical mining represents a signiﬁcant source of con-
tamination to the ﬂuvial system (e.g., Hudson-Edwards et al., 1999;
Coulthard and Macklin, 2003; Dennis et al., 2009; Beane et al., 2016;
Bird,
2016). Individualﬂood events can transport substantial quantities
of contaminated sediment downstream, impacting important agri-
cultural land and potentially contributing to livestock poisoning and
increased mortality (Foulds et al., 2014). Germany has a history of

__data__.text:
mining that extends back centuries. Some of the earliest activity has
been traced to around 3500 yr BP in the Harz Mountains of central
Germany (Matschullat et al., 1997;Monna et al., 2000). Other regions
with a long history of mining include Rammelsberg (Matschullat et al.,
1997; Brännvall et al., 1999; Bindler et al., 2011) and eastern Bavaria
(Hürkamp et al., 2009;Raab et al., 2011). Early mining activity was
relatively ineﬃcient in extracting and processing materials, typically
leaving behind large quantities of trace metals that could be conveyed
to downstreamﬂoodplains. Today contaminants stored inﬂoodplain
sediments provide an“archive” of past mining activity and the resultant
metal contamination (Hürkamp et al., 2009). Vertical trends in trace
metals can be useful in documenting the movement of metal-con-
taminated sediments through drainage basins and assessing the poten-
tial for near-channelﬂoodplain sediments to serve as future sources of
downstream contamination (Gocht et al., 2001; Middelkoop, 2002;
Vallius, 2014;Lecce and Pavlowsky, 2014).
Studies of the distribution of trace metals around and downstream
from mines have established typical spatial patterns for metal con-
tamination. Floodplain sediments and channel banks have been shown
to contain elevated metal concentrations tens of kilometers downstream
from former mines (Coulthard and Macklin, 2003; Dennis et al., 2009;
Foulds et al., 2014; Lecce and Pavlowsky, 2014; Beane et al., 2016;
Bird, 2016; Wadige et al., 2016; Clement et al., 2017). Metal con-
centrations typically decrease with distance from the former mines,
reﬂecting the additions of cleaner sediments from downstream tribu-
taries and the tendency for metal-contaminated sediments to be de-
posited in close proximity to the mine. Trace metals stored inﬂoodplain
sediments from prior mining activity are regarded aslegacy sediments
(James, 2013) that have the potential of serving as sources for future
metal contamination (Leigh, 1994;Schwartz et al., 2006;Ciszewski and
Turner, 2009; Dennis et al., 2009;Wyżga and Ciszewski, 2010;Foulds
et al., 2014; Bird, 2016; Wadige et al., 2016).
I previously documented storage of trace metals inﬂoodplain se-
diments and changes in metal concentrations over time along the Lahn
River, a predominantly agricultural watershed of ~5000 km2 in west-
central Germany (Martin, 2009, 2012). The 25-km reach of the lower
Lahn River between Wetzlar and Weilburg was found to have the
highest metal concentrations (Martin, 2012). This was attributed to the
input of contaminated sediments by the Dill River, a tributary that
empties into the Lahn River at Wetzlar. To assess the potential con-
tribution of trace metals from the Dill River to the lower Lahn River, I
examined anthropogenic enrichment of trace metals inﬂoodplain se-
diments along a 25-km reach of the lower Dill River, documenting that
near-channel sediments are enriched with trace metals (Martin, 2015).
The potential source of trace metals in the lower Dill River is either
heavy industry in the upper Dill River basin (Fröhlich et al., 2008)o r
past mining activity (Meyer, 2007).
To assess the contribution of formerly mined areas to the elevated
metal concentrations along the lower Dill and Lahn Rivers, I focus here
on 9 tributaries whose headwaters are in the vicinity of former mines
(Fig. 1). Four of the tributaries drain to the lower Lahn River andﬁve to
the lower Dill River. The earliest mention of mining in the region is 780
(Wenzel, 2003).

__data__.text:
The potential source of trace metals in the lower Dill River is either
heavy industry in the upper Dill River basin (Fröhlich et al., 2008)o r
past mining activity (Meyer, 2007).
To assess the contribution of formerly mined areas to the elevated
metal concentrations along the lower Dill and Lahn Rivers, I focus here
on 9 tributaries whose headwaters are in the vicinity of former mines
(Fig. 1). Four of the tributaries drain to the lower Lahn River andﬁve to
the lower Dill River. The earliest mention of mining in the region is 780
(Wenzel, 2003). Peak mining activity occurred between 1850 and the
mid-1870s and from the early 1900s to the 1930s (Wenzel, 2003;
Meyer, 2007). Following World War II, mining in the region declined,
with the last mine (the Grube Fortuna iron mine) closing in 1983
(Wenzel, 2003; Meyer, 2007). Within the broad goal of assessing the
contribution of formerly mined areas to trace metal concentrations
along the lower Lahn and Dill Rivers, the speciﬁc objectives of this
research are to (i) document metal concentration at near-channel sites
along tributaries that drain formerly mined areas and along the lower
Lahn River between Wetzlar and Weilburg, (ii) examine vertical trends
in trace metal concentrations at sample sites, (iii) compare trace metal
concentrations along tributaries to concentrations in the lower Lahn
and Dill Rivers, and (iv) assess the contribution of tributaries to the
elevated metal concentration along the lower Lahn and Dill Rivers.
2. Study area
The Dill River, with headwaters in the Lahn-Dill low mountains of
west-central Germany, drains an area of ca. 700 km2; the Lahn River,
with headwaters in the rural uplands north of Marburg, drains an area
of ca. 5000 km2 (Fig. 1). Unlike the Lahn River, the Dill River has not
been extensively channelized, resulting in higher ﬂow velocity and
stream power than along the Lahn River. Overbankﬂow generally oc-
curs during the winter and early spring (December to April), a period of
higher precipitation and potential snowmelt from upland areas (Breuer
et al., 2009). Slightly > 50% of the Dill River watershed is forested
(mainly uplands), 27% is in agriculture (arable land and pasture), and
10% is urban (Fröhlich et al., 2008; Breuer et al., 2009). Land use in the
Lahn River watershed is 70% agriculture (arable land and pasture),
16% forested, and 14% urban (Jöckel, 1981). Along both rivers, arable
land is typically separated from the channel bank by a ca. 3-m-wide,
near-channel vegetation zone of low-lying brush. The 9 tributary
streams drain uplands adjacent to the lower Dill and Lahn Rivers. Tri-
butaries have steeper altitudinal gradients compared to the gradients
along the lower Dill and Lahn Rivers andﬂow through mainly forested
areas. Along tributaries, slope gradients range from 0.44° to 2.12°, with
the steeper gradients present along tributaries thatﬂow into the lower
Dill River; slope gradients along the lower Dill and Lahn Rivers range
from 0.02° to 0.14°, with steepest gradients found along the lower Dill
River.
Potential sources of trace metals documented in the lower Dill and
Lahn Rivers include former steel mills, where trace metals were used as
alloys in steel manufacture, in the upper part of the Dill River near and
upriver from Herborn (Fröhlich et al., 2008), and the mines that were
once active in uplands of the watershed (Meyer, 2007). Fe ore, but also
Cu and Pb ore, were mined from Carboniferous shale; the same shale
serves as a potential non-anthropogenic source of Cu, Pb, and Zn
(Wetzel, 1994).

__data__.text:
Potential sources of trace metals documented in the lower Dill and
Lahn Rivers include former steel mills, where trace metals were used as
alloys in steel manufacture, in the upper part of the Dill River near and
upriver from Herborn (Fröhlich et al., 2008), and the mines that were
once active in uplands of the watershed (Meyer, 2007). Fe ore, but also
Cu and Pb ore, were mined from Carboniferous shale; the same shale
serves as a potential non-anthropogenic source of Cu, Pb, and Zn
(Wetzel, 1994). Industrial activity represents an alternative source of
trace metals in the basin. Analysis of 73 sites along a 60-km length of
the Dill River revealed maximum concentrations of trace metals in
stream water samples collected immediately downstream from steel
mill locations (Fröhlich et al. (2008). The reach with the highest con-
centrations of trace metals corresponds to the lower Dill River from
Herborn to Wetzlar where I documented anthropogenic storage of Cu,
Pb, and Zn in near-channelﬂoodplains (Martin, 2015).
3. Materials and methods
Through ﬁeld and archival reconnaissance, I selected 9 tributary
streams that drain formerly mined areas. With the exception of large
mines like the Grube Fortuna (Fig. 2), evidence of mining activity from
the generally small mines is often diﬃcult to discern on the modern
landscape, but is portrayed on 1:25,000 topographic maps. Samples
were collected at 15 sites along tributary streams. Samples were also
collected from 7 near-channel sites along the lower Lahn River between
Wetzlar and Weilburg to better document trace metal concentrations
there. Generally, sites were located at an interval of every 2– 4 km along
the lower Lahn River and every 1 km along tributary streams to ensure
systematic coverage while avoiding potential sources of trace metals
such as major roads, rail lines, and industrial facilities. Every attempt
was made to select an equal number of left and right channel bank sites,
although limited channel access made this diﬃcult in a few reaches.
The geographical latitude and longitude of each sample site was re-
corded using a hand-held GPS unit.
At each sample site, I collected a 2.5 cm diameter core using an
Oakﬁeld handheld corer. Cores were collected from near-channel se-
diments to a depth of at least 1.0 m along the lower Lahn and to a depth
of ca. 0.6 m along tributaries. Coarse grained and rocky sub-surface
materials prevented deeper coring at some tributary sites. In theﬁeld,
cores were sampled at an interval of 5 cm for analysis of trace metals
and
standard sediment analyses. Samples were stored in sterile plastic

__data__.text:
bags and transported to the geomorphology lab at Justus-Liebig
Universität in Giessen. In the lab, each sample was split, with half re-
tained for grain size analysis and organic matter content determination
and half submitted to a commercial laboratory for analysis of trace
metals. At the lab, samples were sieved to separate the < 63μm frac-
tion on which trace metal analysis was completed. Trace metals are
most often transported and stored on the < 63μm fraction (Ntekim
et al., 1993;Mantei and Sappington, 1994; Foster and Charlesworth,
1996; Owens et al., 2005); using this fraction also provides consistency
with my previous research along the Lahn and Dill Rivers. Samples
wereﬁrst digested in percholoric, nitric, and hydroﬂuoric acids (triple-
acid digestion), a process that has been found to yield nearly total re-
covery of trace metals (Lecce and Pavlowsky, 1997). The concentra-
tions of Cu, Pb, and Zn were measured using inductively coupled
plasma atomic emission spectroscopy (ICE-AES). The analytical sensi-
tivity was 1.0 mg kg−1 for Cu and 2.0 mg kg−1 for Pb and Zn. Quality
control information provided by the laboratory yielded coeﬃcients of
variation on duplicate samples of 2.3% for Cu, 3.7% for Pb, and 1.5%
for Zn. Repeated measurements of standards by the lab produced
coeﬃcients of variation of 1.8% for Cu, 2.6% for Pb, and 2.0% for Zn.
On the half of samples that I retained in the lab, the pipette method was
used on 10 g samples to determine the proportions of clay (< 2μm) and
silt (2– 62 μm); the percent sand was determined by wet sieving. Loss on
ignition (LOI) on 3 g samples at 430o C for 24 h yielded organic matter
content (Davies, 1974).
Deeply buried sediments were collected to provide background
trace metal concentrations. Based on vertical metal trends and AMS
radiocarbon ages on charcoal from sediment cores in the Dill River
(Martin, 2015), sediments at depths > 0.6 m date to the pre- or early-
industrial period (early 19th century and older), and are assumed to
provide background trace metal concentrations in the study area.
Background trace metal concentrations are derived from 27 background
samples collected at depths between 0.60 and 1.4 m along the lower
Lahn and Dill Rivers. Determining background (sometimes referred to
as non-anthropogenic) trace metal concentrations can be problematic
(Birch et al., 2000; Matschullat et al., 2000; Bindler et al., 2011).
Matschullat et al. (2000) summarize and assess the options for de-
termining background trace metal concentrations.
To assess the extent of metal contamination, trace metal con-
centrations from sediment cores were compared to standards contained
in the 1998 German Federal Soil Protection Act ( Bundes-
Bodenschutzgesetz {BbodSchG})and the German Federal Soil Protection
and Contaminated Site Ordinance of 1999 (Bundes-
Bodenschutzverordnung{BbodSchV}). These federal acts set trace metal
concentrations above which the“natural soil functions” are thought to
be at risk (the‘precautionary value’). Values are reported for loam/silt
soils and are given in mg kg−1 dry mass ﬁne soil. In addition to stan-
dards provided in the German Federal Protection Act, I compared trace
metal concentrations to the threshold eﬀect concentrations (TEC) and
probable eﬀect concentrations (PEC) ofMacDonald et al. (2000). When
concentrations are less than the TEC, adverse impacts are unlikely; with
concentrations above the PEC, negative impacts are deemed likely.

4.1.

concentrations above which the“natural soil functions” are thought to
be at risk (the‘precautionary value’). Values are reported for loam/silt
soils and are given in mg kg−1 dry mass ﬁne soil. In addition to stan-

4. Results
4.1. Summary metal concentrations
The descriptive statistics for core samples and background samples
from tributaries, the lower Lahn River, and the lower Dill River are
summarized in Table 1. Results from a Mann-WhitneyU Test indicate
that the median concentrations of Cu, Pb, and Zn from tributaries to
both the lower Lahn and Dill Rivers are statistically diﬀerent than
median concentrations for the respective rivers into which the tribu-
taries empty. Mean concentrations along the tributaries are virtually
identical to background concentrations for the lower Lahn and Dill
Rivers. Mean concentrations of Cu, Pb, and Zn are far less than the
precautionary value contained in the German Federal Soil Protection
and Contaminated Site Ordinance of 1999 and the TEC and PEC levels
of MacDonald et al. (2000). Along tributaries that drain into the Dill
River, a few individual samples (as reﬂected in the range of con-
centrations) exceed the precautionary and TEC values for Cu and Zn

most contaminated individual sites, as indicated by the maximum

4.2. Vertical trace metal trends
Vertical metal trends from individual cores reﬂect the quantity of
contaminated sediments that have moved through and been deposited
along rivers. Although post-depositional translocation of metals is
possible, especially for those that are less strongly bound to sediments
(Hudson-Edwards et al., 1999), similar“down-core trends”for diﬀerent
trace metals indicate minimal post-depositional mobilization (Lecce
and Pavlowsky 2014, 126–128). Vertical trends in trace metals and
percent silt and clay from representative cores collected along tributary
streams are shown inFig. 3; vertical trends from other tributary cores
are shown in Supplementary materials. Two letter designations refer to
the tributary name (e.g., LP-Lempbach) or nearby geographic location
(e.g., GF - Grube Fortuna mine). Numbers reﬂect the position along the
tributary, with higher numbers positioned farther downstream. Peaks in
trace metal concentrations are present at speciﬁc depths below the
surface at several tributary sites, but are less pronounced than along the
lower Dill River (Martin, 2015). In addition, the range of metal con-
centrations along tributaries is far less than the range from the lower
Dill River (Table 1). The depth of peak concentrations varies widely
from 0 to 0.45 m for Cu, Pb, and Zn. For those cores where the peak
concentration occurs at a single depth, the mean depths of the peak
concentrations (and standard deviations) for Cu, Pb, and Zn are 0.20
(0.17), 0.12 (0.15), and 0.06 m (0.09), respectively (n=1 0). Vertical
trends for percent silt and clay reveal no relationship between sediment
grain size and trace metal concentrations.
In contrast to vertical metal trends noted along tributary streams,
the trends in cores collected along the lower Lahn River (Fig. 4) are
similar to trends previously reported along the Dill River (Martin,
2015); additional vertical trends are shown in Supplementary mate-
rials. Most cores along the lower Lahn River display a pronounced
single peak in metal concentrations at depths between 0.2 and 0.5 m. In
individual cores, the vertical trends for the three trace metals are
generally similar, suggesting minimal post-depositional migration of
metals. For those cores along the lower Lahn River where the peak
concentration occurs at a single depth, the mean depths of the peak
concentrations (and standard deviations) for Cu, Pb, and Zn are 0.29
(0.09), 0.33 (0.17), and 0.29 m (0.09), respectively (n=5 ), similar to
what was noted along the lower Dill River (Martin, 2015). Along the
lower Lahn River, there is no systematic diﬀerence in vertical trends
and trace metal concentrations with distance downstream from the
conﬂuence of the Dill and Lahn Rivers in Wetzlar (Fig. 4). Sediments
deposited most recently (in the upper 0.40 m of cores) are less con-
taminated with trace metals than sediments lower in the cores, an in-
dication that cleaner sediments have begun to move through the lower
Lahn River during the last several decades. Similar declines in metal
concentrations in ﬂoodplain sediments have been noted elsewhere in
western Europe (e.g.,Brügmann, 1995;Zerling et al., 2006; Zachmann
et al., 2013; Schillereﬀ et al., 2016 ).
4.3. Tributary stream metal concentrations
The concentrations of trace metals in near-channel positions along
tributary streams are less than concentrations along the lower Dill and
Lahn Rivers.

4.3. Tributary stream metal concentrations
The concentrations of trace metals in near-channel positions along
tributary streams are less than concentrations along the lower Dill and
Lahn Rivers. Mean concentrations along theﬁve Dill tributaries for Cu,
Pb, and Zn are 36%, 29%, and 31%, respectively, of the means for those
trace metals along the lower Dill River; mean concentrations along the
four Lahn tributaries for Cu, Pb, and Zn are 33%, 28%, and 24%, re-
spectively, of the means for those trace metals along the lower Lahn
River. The maximum values for the three trace metals noted along the
ﬁve tributary streams to the Dill River range from 17% (Zn) to 25%
(Cu) of the maximum concentrations noted along the lower Dill River;
maximum values for the three trace metals noted along four tributary
streams to the Lahn River range from 13% (Pb) to 28% (Cu) of the
maximum concentrations noted along the lower Lahn River. Box plots
of the median and mean values for the tributary streams vs. the lower
Dill and Lahn Rivers illustrate the diﬀerence in metal concentrations
(Fig. 5).
5. Discussion
Cores collected along tributary streams suggest that large quantities
of Cu, Pb, and Zn from upstream mining activity are not present in near-
channel positions. Some vertical variation in trace metal concentrations
exists, but diﬀerences between peak concentrations and minimum va-
lues are small. Given that trace metals are often found in association
withﬁne-grained sediments (Horowitz, 1985;Foster and Charlesworth,
1996; Owens et al., 2005), the low metal concentrations could be ex-
plained by absence ofﬁne-grained sediments along the relatively steep-
gradient tributary streams. A lack ofﬁne-grained sediments along tri-
butaries is not, however, supported by grain-size data from 56 samples
collected along the tributaries. These samples reveal that sediments are
predominantly ﬁne-grained, with the mean percentage of silt and clay
at 86.9% (standard deviation of 9.2%). Rather than being a function of
the grain size of sediments, the low concentrations of Cu, Pb, and Zn
along tributaries indicate that metal-contaminated sediments are not
present.
The absence of high concentrations of trace metals along tributaries
is surprising given the long history of Fe, Cu, and Pb mining in the study
area. Perhaps the mining process did not release signiﬁcant quantities
of metals to tributaries, although studies of mined watersheds else-
where in Germany (e.g.,Matschullat et al., 1997;Monna et al., 2000;
Hürkamp et al., 2009 ) and western Europe (e.g., Coulthard and
Macklin, 2003; Beane et al., 2016; Bird, 2016) found signiﬁcant levels
of metals stored along rivers immediately downstream from mines.
Contaminated sediments may have been conveyed through, rather than
stored along, the relatively high gradient tributaries to the lower Dill
and Lahn Rivers; gradients along tributary streams are much greater
than gradients along the lower Dill and Lahn Rivers, although the
maximum gradient found along tributaries to the Dill (2.12°) is still

relatively low. If metals had been moved through rather than deposited
along tributary streams, relatively high concentrations of metals might
be expected in cores collected close to the mouth of tributaries where
stream gradient, and thus stream power, decrease. In addition, tributary
ﬂoodplains are wider in the lower reaches, which would favor deposi-
tion. Samples taken from the most downstream sites along tributaries
(Fig. 3 - GF3(17), LP2) do not have higher metal concentrations than
samples collected upstream, suggesting that higher concentrations of
metals were either 1) released to tributaries and then conveyed directly
to the main channel, or 2) never transported through tributary streams.
If metals had been released to tributaries, but subsequently trans-
ported downstream through them to the main valleys, cores collected
along ﬂoodplains of the lower Dill and Lahn Rivers immediately
downstream of tributary conﬂuences with the main channel might be
expected to have higher concentrations of trace metals thanﬂoodplains
immediately upstream of conﬂuences. The maximum and mean metal
concentrations for each sample site along the lower Dill and Lahn
Rivers and the locations where each tributary enters the main channel
do not consistently reveal higher concentrations immediately down-
stream from tributary conﬂuences (Fig. 6). The spatial pattern of trace
metals along the main channelﬂoodplains of the lower Dill and Lahn
Rivers is not consistent with tributaries contributing large quantities of
trace metals.
It appears that mined areas have not served as an important source
for anthropogenic metals found along the lower Dill and Lahn Rivers,
perhaps because mining did not release large quantities of metals to the
ﬂuvial environment. Cores show minimal trace metal concentrations in
tributary ﬂoodplain sediments, meaning there is little risk that sedi-
ments stored along tributaries will serve as a future source of down-
stream trace metal contamination. Instead, elevated anthropogenic
concentrations of metals along the lower Lahn River appear to have
originated from industrial sources such as those noted in the upper Dill
River byFröhlich et al. (2008). The peak metal concentrations in cores
collected along the lower Lahn River are assumed to correspond to, or
directly follow, maximum metal releases to the environment. Industrial
activity in the upper Dill River is ongoing, but the peak period of ac-
tivity, and likely period of less restrictive environmental regulations,
occurred from the mid-1800s to the mid-1900s (Fröhlich et al., 2008).
This timeline of the expansion and contraction of industrial activity has
been noted elsewhere in studies that document the input of trace metals

Schulte et al., 1996;Renberg et al., 2001;De Vleeschouwer et al., 2007;
Baborowski and Einax, 2016; Dhivert et al., 2016;Horák and Hejeman,

AMS radiocarbon ages on charcoal from alluvium along the lower
Dill River indicate that sediments with peak concentrations of metals
were deposited after the mid/late seventeenth century, with several
sites displaying peak metal concentrations at 100 to 150 years ago
(Martin, 2015). Assuming the alluvial stratigraphy along the lower
Lahn River is coeval with that along the lower Dill River, the peak metal
concentrations at ca. 0.30 m date to the late 1800s and early 1900s. The
releases of pollutants by industrial activities to the environment has
lessened over recent decades as indicated by vertical trends from the
lower Dill (Martin, 2015) and Lahn Rivers (Fig. 4) showing up-core
declines in metal concentrations. Although recently-deposited sedi-
ments are cleaner, near-channel sediments along the lower Dill and
Lahn Rivers still contain metal-contaminated sediments that may serve
as potential sources of downstream trace metal pollution in the fore-
seeable future as has been noted in other western European watersheds
(e.g., Förstner, 2003; Krüger et al., 2005;Macklin et al., 2006;Foulds
et al., 2014; Resongles et al., 2014).
6. Conclusions
A century of mining in uplands adjacent to the lower Dill and Lahn
Rivers of central Germany does not appear to have contributed trace
metals toﬂoodplain sediments of tributaries. Concentrations of Cu, Pb,
and Zn in cores collected from 9 tributary streams that empty into the
lower Dill River or Lahn River diﬀer little from background metal
concentrations and are signiﬁcantly less than trace metal concentra-
tions from near-channel sediments along the lower Dill and Lahn
Rivers. Mean concentrations of Cu, Pb, and Zn are below the precau-
tionary value contained in the German Federal Soil Protection Act and
the TEC and PEC values ofMacDonald et al. (2000), although some
individual samples exceed the precautionary and TEC values. Vertical
metal trends in tributary cores reveal peak concentrations at depth
below the surface, but peak concentrations diﬀer little from minimum
concentrations in the majority of cores, typically by a factor of only 1.5
to 2.0. Peak concentrations in tributary cores are far less than peak
concentrations in cores extracted from the lower Dill River and lower
Lahn River. The metals along the lower Lahn and Dill Rivers appear to
have been derived from upstream industrial activity in cities such as
Herborn and Dillenburg (Fröhlich et al., 2008).
This study serves as an example of an historically mined area not
contributing to anthropogenic concentrations of trace metals found in
downstream near-channel locations. Perhaps because the mines were
generally small, the mining and processing of ore did not leave large
quantities of contaminated materials exposed on the landscape where
they could be transported to watersheds. It appears that the former
mines and streams that drain them have a very low potential of serving
as sources for metals to downstream rivers in the near future.
Downstream water andﬂoodplain soil quality do not appear to be en-
dangered by the contribution of trace metals from upland mined areas.
At the same time, relatively high concentrations of Cu, Pb, and Zn are
stored in near-channel positions along the lower Lahn River as well as
along the lower Dill River. Channel bank erosion has the potential of
entraining these metal-contaminated sediments and transporting them
downstream. Given the high concentrations of metals present along the
lower Dill River, the lower Lahn River into which the Dill empties at

Trace metal storage in recentﬂoodplain sediments along the Dill River,
central Germany
Charles W. Martin⁎
Department of Geography, 118 Seaton Hall, Kansas State University, Manhattan, KS 66506-2904, USA
abstractarticle info
Article history:
Received 9 August 2014
Received in revised form 23 January 2015
Accepted 27 January 2015
Available online 7 February 2015
Keywords:
Trace metals
Recent ﬂoodplain sedimentation
Industrial/mined watersheds
Sediment contamination
Germany
Trace metals are stored in near-channelﬂoodplain sediments along many rivers in industrial and mined water-
sheds of western European countries such as Germany. In this paper, I document the distribution of Cu, Pb, and Zn
in 13 cores collected from near-channelﬂoodplain sediments along a 25-km reach of the Dill River in central
Germany. Mean concentrations of the three trace metals exceed background concentrations, an indication of
anthropogenic enrichment along the study reach; many individual samples have concentrations several times
the background levels and exceed standards for trace metals contained in the German Federal Soil Protection
Act. Metal concentrations generally peak at depths of 0.2 to 0.7 m below theﬂoodplain surface and are assumed
to represent the period of maximum metal releases to the environment through upstream industrial activity, ore
mining, or both. In eight of the cores, radiocarbon ages obtained below the depth of peak metal concentrations
provide maximum dates for sediment accumulation of between 90 and 1700 years ago, with most ages clustering
in the period of 90 to 300 years ago. The ages and depth to peak metal concentrations indicate 0.6 to 1.0 m of
ﬂoodplain sedimentation over the last 150 to 300 years (0.3–0.4 cm y−1), which exceed sedimentation amounts
and rates found in surrounding watersheds. Surface sediments contain lower metal concentrations, suggesting
deposition recently of cleaner sediments. Trace metals stored along the Dill River serve as a reminder that stores
of contaminants exist in geomorphically sensitive locations of theﬂuvial system. Theselegacysediments bear the
chemical imprint of industrial or mining activities that no longer occur in the watershed.

1. Introduction
Contamination with trace metals is widespread in numerous
watersheds worldwide. The source of the metals varies but often
can be linked to industrial activity, agriculture, mining, or a combina-
tion thereof. In areas such as western Europe, metals have been
discharged to the environment for centuries ( Matschullat et al.,
1997; Brännvall et al., 1999; Renberg et al., 2001), although the
maximum releases generally occurred between the mid-nineteenth
century and early 1970s (Valette-Silver, 1993; Renberg et al., 2001;
Middelkoop, 2002; De Vleeschouwer et al., 2007). The earliest source
of trace metal contamination is mining, which in parts of Europe
extends back more than 3000 years (Monna et al., 2000). Many stud-
ies have documented the long-term environmental impacts of metal
storage in, and conveyance through, mined and industrial water-
sheds (Leigh, 1994, 1997; Miller, 1997; Macklin et al. 2006; Bábek
et al., 2008; Lecce et al., 2008; Foulds et al., 2014; Lecce and
Pavlowsky, 2014; Resongles et al., 2014). Trace metals impact the
ﬂuvial environment in many ways, including water quality, aquatic
ecosystems, and the health of humans ( Lecce and Pavlowsky,
2014). Although mining ceased in many contaminated watersheds de-
cades earlier, debris generated by the mining process is stored asﬂood-
plain and channel sediments, serving as a source for trace metal
pollution downstream.

Pavlowsky, 2014; Resongles et al., 2014). Trace metals impact the
ﬂuvial environment in many ways, including water quality, aquatic
ecosystems, and the health of humans ( Lecce and Pavlowsky,
2014). Although mining ceased in many contaminated watersheds de-
cades earlier, debris generated by the mining process is stored asﬂood-
plain and channel sediments, serving as a source for trace metal
pollution downstream. When metals are stored in geomorphically sensi-
tive areas such as channel banks or near-channel positions, they may be
readily remobilized and conveyed downstream by multiple or single
events (James, 1989; Marcus, 1989; Leigh, 1997; Förstner, 2003; Krüger
et al., 2005; Foulds et al., 2014).
In western Europe, the impact of past mining onﬂoodplain and chan-
nel bank sediments has been well documented (Hudson-Edwards et al.,
1999; Mascaro et al., 2001; Coulthard and Macklin, 2003; Hürkamp
et al., 2009; Resongles et al., 2014). Trace metal contamination has been
noted in ﬂoodplain sediments and channel banks tens of kilometers
below historically mined reaches of watersheds. Frequently, metal
concentrations decrease with distance from the former mines, a trend
usually attributed to deposition of a majority of metals in close proximity
to the mined areas and the addition of cleaner sediments from down-
stream tributaries. Highly contaminated channel banks and near-
channel ﬂoodplain sediments have been shown to serve as a source for
metal contamination duringﬂoods (Leigh, 1994; Schwartz et al., 2006;
Ciszewski and Turner, 2009; Wyżga and Ciszewski, 2010; Foulds et al.,
2014). Industrial activity can also serve as a source of trace metals, as
has been documented in western Europe along rivers such as the Rhine

__data__.text:

(Förstner, 2003, Krüger and Gröngröft, 2003; Schulz-Zunkel et al., 2013;
Zachmann et al., 2013).
Work that I have undertaken since the mid-1990s along the Lahn
River, a predominantly agricultural watershed of ~5000 km2 in west-
central Germany, served as the impetus for the present study (Fig. 1).
My previous research documents anthropogenic trace metal storage
inﬂoodplain sediments along a 75-km reach of the Lahn River, exam-
ining the geographic pattern of trace metal storage across theﬂood-
plain (Martin, 1997, 2000) and the change in near-channel storage of
trace metals since the mid-1990s (Martin, 2009, 2012). Along the
Lahn River downstream of its con ﬂuence with the Dill River in
Wetzlar, trace metal concentrations increase ( Martin, 2012 ).
Although the Lahn River has no history of mining upstream of
Wetzlar, mining operations were present in the Lahn River down-
stream from Wetzlar and in the upper Dill River from the 1830s
until the last mine closed in 1983; the peak of mining activity in
the Dill and lower Lahn Rivervalleys was between 1870 and 1945
(Meyer, 2007). Historically, steel mills also operated in the upper
part of the Dill River watershed (Fröhlich et al., 2008). Preliminary
sampling of channel banks along the Dill River revealed Cu, Pb,
and Zn concentrations above those found in similar geomorphic
positions along the Lahn River (Martin, 2012). The research reported
here focuses on trace metal storage in additional near-channel sites
along a 25-km reach of the Dill River and uses trace metal vertical
trends and radiocarbon ages to document recent ﬂoodplain
sedimentation.
The impact of historical mining activity on rivers and streams has
been extensively documented in the UK (e.g.,Hudson-Edwards et al.,
1999; Coulthard and Macklin, 2003; Dennis et al., 2009; Foulds et al.,
2014). In Germany, mining extends back many centuries, with some
of the oldest documented activity dating to around 3500 Y BP in the
Harz Mountains of central Germany (Matschullat et al., 1997; Monna
et al., 2000). A signiﬁcant expansion of mining occurred there in AD
980 with the establishment of the Rammelsberg mines (Matschullat
et al., 1997; Brännvall et al., 1999; Bindler et al., 2011). The northern
Vils River of eastern Bavaria, where mining began about 1000 Y BP, is
another area of early historical mining in Germany (Hürkamp et al.,
2009). Typically, mining released large quantities of trace metals to
the environment that were subsequently conveyed downstream and
stored inﬂoodplains. Today, they provide anarchive of past mining
activity and the resultant metal contamination (Hürkamp et al., 2009).
Vertical trends in trace metals, which have been used to document
movement of metal-contaminated sediments through drainage basins,
permit assessment of the potential for near-channelﬂoodplain sedi-
ments to serve as future sources of downstream contamination (Gocht
et al., 2001; Middelkoop, 2002; Lecce and Pavlowsky, 2014; Vallius,
2014). When age control on vertical metal trends is available, either

__data__.text:
through knowledge of the upstream industrial or mining history or
through radiometric ages, calculation of recent overbank sedimentation
rates is possible (Krüger et al., 2006; Lecce et al., 2008; Matys Grygar
et al., 2011; Lecce and Pavlowsky, 2014; Resongles et al., 2014).
In central Germany, the late Holocene alluvial record has been
compiled on a timescale of thousands of years (Lang and Nolte,
1999; Rittweger, 2000; Bos and Urz, 2003; Houben, 2003, 2012;
Kalis et al., 2003; Wennrich at al., 2005; Hoffmann et al., 2007), but
an understanding of alluvial sedimentation rates over shorter time-
scales of hundreds of years is lacking. The present study provides
new information on alluvial sedimentation over the last 300 years
using trace metal trends and radiocarbon ages on stratigraphy. With-
in the broad goal of examining trace metal storage in near-channel
ﬂoodplain sediments of the Dill River, the speciﬁco b j e c t i v e so ft h i s
research are to (i) document the extent of trace metal storage in
near-channel ﬂoodplain sediments along a 25-km reach of the Dill
River from Herborn to the mouth of the river at Wetzlar; (ii) examine
the vertical trends in trace metal concentrations at the near-channel
sites; (iii) using radiocarbon ages and vertical trace metal trends,
estimate recent ﬂoodplain sedimentation rates; and (iv) compare
trace metal concentrations in the Dill River valley with concentra-
tions in the adjacent Lahn River valley upstream from the conﬂuence
of the two rivers.
2. Study area
The Dill River, with headwaters in the Lahn–Dill low mountain range
of west-central Germany, drains an area of ca. 700 km2 (Fig. 1). Along its
length, the river drops from 700 to 150 m,ﬂowing straight southward
through the cities of Dillenburg and Herborn for a distance of nearly
60 km before emptying into the Lahn River at Wetzlar. Unlike the
Lahn River, the Dill River has not been extensively channelized,
resulting in higherﬂow velocity and stream power than along the
Lahn River. Overbank ﬂow generally occurs during the winter and
early spring (December to April), a period of higher precipitation and
potential snowmelt from upland areas (Breuer et al., 2009). The litholo-
gy of the Dill basin is highly variable, with Tertiary metabasalts and
greenstone in the upper and lowermost parts of the study reach and
Carboniferous siltstone and shale in the middle portion (Fröhlich et al.,
2008). Slightly more than 50% of the watershed is forested (mainly
uplands) and 20% is in pasture (lowlands andﬂoodplain), with small
amounts of arable land (7%) in the southern-most part of the study
reach (Fröhlich et al., 2008; Breuer et al., 2009). Arable land is typically
separated from the channel bank by a ca. 3-m-wide, near-channel
vegetation zone of low-lying brush. Urban areas constitute nearly 10%
of the basin area, primarily adjacent to the Dill River in the lower two-
thirds of the basin (Breuer et al., 2009). Watershed characteristics are
provided inTable 1.
The ﬂoodplain is underlain by late Holocene (last 3000 years)
alluvium and colluvium whose thickness in the adjacent Lahn and
Wetter River basins ranges from 2.5–3 m in the Lahn watershed
(Rittweger, 2000; Bos and Urz, 2003)t o1–2 m in the Wetter drain-
age basin (Houben, 2003).

(Rittweger, 2000; Bos and Urz, 2003)t o1–2 m in the Wetter drain-
age basin (Houben, 2003). Research along the Lahn River suggests
that ﬂoodplain alluvium accumulated during the late Holocene
when the forest cover on surrounding uplands was removed for
timber or cultivation, accelerating hillslope erosion and transporting
sediment to the valley ﬂoor (Rittweger, 2000; Kalis et al., 2003;
Hoffmann et al., 2007). Inceptisols are the most common USDA soil
taxonomy type in the watershed, occupying nearly two-thirds of
the catchment area (Breuer et al., 2009).
Potential sources of trace metals include former steel mills—where
trace metals were used as alloys in steel manufacture in the upper part
of the 25-km study reach near and upstream from Herborn (Fröhlich
et al., 2008)—a n dt h em i n e st h a tw e r eo n c ea c t i v ei nu p l a n d so ft h ew a t e r -
shed (Meyer, 2007). Mining in the upper Dill River and lower Lahn River
dates back many hundreds of years, but the peak period of mining was
from 1870 to 1945; the last mine in the Dill and lower Lahn River basins,
the Grube Fortuna iron mine, closed in 1983 (Meyer, 2007). Chieﬂyi r o n
ore, but also some copper and lead ore, were mined in the Dill and
lower Lahn River basins from Carboniferous shale; this same shale serves
as a potential nonanthropogenic source of Cu, Pb, and Zn in the study
reach (Wetzel, 1994). Industrial activity represents an additional possible
source of trace metals in the basin. Through analysis of 73 streamwater
sites along the entire 60 km length of the Dill River,Fröhlich et al.
(2008) found maximum concentrations of trace metals in samples
collected immediately downstream from steel mill locations. The reach
where water samples contained the highest concentrations of trace
metals corresponds to the 25-km reach of the Dill River examined in
this study.
3. Methods
Through ﬁeld reconnaissance, I selected 13 near-channel (b5m
from the active channel) sites along a 25-km reach of the Dill River
between Herborn and Wetzlar. Sites were chosen at an interval of
every 2–4 km along the river to ensure systematic coverage along the
study reach while at that same time avoiding major roads, rail lines,
and industrial facilities. Every attempt was made to select an equal
number of left and right channel bank sites, although limited channel
access made this difﬁcult in a few reaches. The geographical latitude
and longitude of each sample site was recorded using a hand-held
GPS unit. Sample locations are shown onFig. 1.
At each sample site, I collected a 2.5-cm diameter core fromﬂood-
plain sediments using an Oakﬁeld handheld corer to a depth of at least
1.0 m. In theﬁeld, cores were sampled at an interval of 5 cm for analysis
of trace metals and standard sediment analyses. Samples were stored in
sterile plastic bags and transported to the geomorphology lab at Justus-
Liebig Universität in Giessen, where each sample was split, with half
retained for grain size analysis and organic matter content determina-
tion and half submitted to ALS Chemex Labs (an ISO 902 registered an-
alytical laboratory in North America) for analysis of trace metals.

used to determine the proportions of clay (b2 μm) and silt (2–62 μm);

Samples collected at depths of 0.65 to 1.10 m were used to
determine the background, or pre-industrial (pre-1750 A.D.), concen-
trations of trace metals. Concentrations in the background samples
were then compared to concentrations in samples collected from the
sediment cores to establish the degree of trace metal enrichment. As
noted in previous research (e.g.,Birch et al., 2000; Matschullat et al.,
2000; Bindler et al., 2011), determining pre-industrial (sometimes re-
ferred to as nonanthropogenic) trace metal concentrations is problem-
atic. Matschullat et al. (2000)summarized and assessed the options for
determining background trace metal concentrations, including the
use of global trace metal data as opposed to locally or regionally ob-
tained background values. As I have done in previous work along the
Lahn River (Martin, 2000, 2012), deeply buried sediments were col-
lected and analyzed for trace metal concentrations to yield back-
ground values. Based on vertical metal trends and AMS radiocarbon
ages on charcoal from sedimentcores, sediments at depthsN0.6 m
date to the pre- or early-industrial period (early nineteenth century
and older), and therefore are assumed to provide an accurate indica-
tion of background trace metal concentrations in the study area. In
total, 19 samples provided background concentrations of Cu, Pb,
and Zn.
To assess the degree of contamination, trace metal concentrations
from sediment cores were compared to standards contained in the
1998 German Federal Soil Protection Act (Bundes-Bodenschutzgesetz
{BbodSchG}) and the German Federal Soil Protection and Contaminated
Site Ordinance of 1999 (Bundes-Bodenschutzverordnung {BbodSchV}).
These federal acts spell out the trace metal concentration above which
the ‘natural soil functions’ are thought to be at risk (the‘precautionary
value’). Values are reported for loam/silt soils and are given in mg kg−1
dry weightﬁne soil. I used threshold effect concentrations (TEC) and
probable effect concentrations (PEC) outlined byMacDonald et al.
(2000) as an additional measure to assess the degree of trace metal
contamination. At concentrations less than the TEC, adverse impacts are
unlikely; concentrations above the PEC indicate that negative impacts
are likely.
Age control on sediment cores was afforded by radiocarbon ages
on charcoal fragments recovered at several sample sites. In 8 of the
13 sediment cores, charcoal was recovered at depths ranging from
0.49 to 1.10 m. Charcoal was stored in sterile plastic bags andﬁrst
refrigerated in the geomorphology lab at Giessen and later in the
Paleoenvironmental lab of the Department of Geography at Kansas
State University. Charcoal was s ubmitted to Beta Analytic, Inc.
for standard AMS radiocarbon dating. Dates on the charcoal pro-
vide age control on alluvial stratigraphy and an independent veriﬁ-
cation of the timing of trace metal accumulation in ﬂoodplain
sediments.
Although regarded as suitable for radiocarbon dating (Pessenda
et al., 2001; Hajdas et al., 2007; Higham at al., 2009), charcoal has
potential limitations when used to date alluvial stratigraphy.

In 8 of the
13 sediment cores, charcoal was recovered at depths ranging from
0.49 to 1.10 m. Charcoal was stored in sterile plastic bags andﬁrst
refrigerated in the geomorphology lab at Giessen and later in the
Paleoenvironmental lab of the Department of Geography at Kansas
State University. Charcoal was s ubmitted to Beta Analytic, Inc.
for standard AMS radiocarbon dating. Dates on the charcoal pro-
vide age control on alluvial stratigraphy and an independent veriﬁ-
cation of the timing of trace metal accumulation in ﬂoodplain
sediments.
Although regarded as suitable for radiocarbon dating (Pessenda
et al., 2001; Hajdas et al., 2007; Higham at al., 2009), charcoal has
potential limitations when used to date alluvial stratigraphy. Biotur-
bation can result in secondary mixing of charcoal and other organic
materials (Adovasio et al., 1990; Pessenda et al., 2001); charcoal
can be contaminated with secondary carbonate and organic acids,
producing anomalous ages (Alon et al., 2002; Hajdas et al., 2007);
and charcoal can be eroded from older sediments, thereby yielding
an anomalously old age for sedimentation (Kennett et al., 2002;
Seidel and Mäckel, 2007; Hoffmann et al., 2008). To avoid dating
reworked charcoal, I used only charcoal fragments that appeared in
large concentrations rather than as isolated fragments, given that
the latter have a higher potential for being reworked from older
deposits (DeLong and Arnold, 2007).
4. Results
4.1. Mean trace metal concentrations
The descriptive statistics for core samples and background samples
are summarized inTable 2. Mean concentrations of Cu, Pb, and Zn
from the core samples exceed the mean background concentrations.
For the surface samples (upper 0.40 m), which represent sediments
deposited after the onset of mining or industrial activity, a clear majority
(97% for Cu, 94% for Pb, and 95% for Zn) have concentrations that are
greater than the background concentrations. Results from a Mann–
Whitney U-Test for unpaired sample means indicate that the mean
concentrations of Cu, Pb, and Zn for samples from the upper 0.40 m of
the cores (where trace metal concentrations are highest) are signiﬁ-
cantly greater (p = 0.05) than the mean concentrations for the back-
ground samples. For all samples, the mean concentrations of Cu, Pb,
and Zn exceed the precautionary value contained in the German Federal
Soil Protection Act and the TEC (threshold effect concentration), but are
less than the PEC (probable effect concentration) ofMacDonald at al.
(2000). For the surface samples, mean concentrations of Cu, Pb, and
Zn exceed the precautionary value and TEC value, but are less than the
PEC value. For Cu, a clear majority of the surface samples exceed the
precautionary value (96%) and TEC value (98%); only 7% of the surface
samples have Cu concentrations that are greater than the PEC value.
For Pb, 82% of the surface samples exceed the precautionary value and
97% are greater than the TEC value, but only 36% of the surface samples
exceed the PEC value. For Zn, 92% of the surface samples have concen-
trations greater than the precautionary value, 93% have concentrations
that are higher than the TEC, but only 29% exceed the PEC value. As
indicated by the range of Cu, Pb, and Zn values, some individual sample
sites have concentrations that far exceed the precautionary value, PEC,
and TEC.

__data__.text:
downstream along the study reach of the Dill River are shown inFig. 2.
Contrary to previous research, which frequently notes a downstream
distance decay in trace metal concentrations (e.g.,Bubb and Lester,
1996; Leigh, 1997; Miller, 1997; Lecce and Pavlowsky, 2014), the con-
centrations along the study reach generally do not decrease with dis-
tance downstream, with the exception of Pb whose mean and
maximum concentrations decline slightly with distance downstream.
As ther2 and p values inFig. 2attest, the statistical relationship between
distance downstream and trace metal concentrations is very weak, at
best. Moving downstream, concentrations of Cu, Pb, and Zn vary in a
nonsystematic fashion, with high mean and maximum concentrations
present throughout the study reach. The absence of a decline in trace
metals with distance downstream may be attributable to several non-
point sources rather than a single point source for contaminants
(Lecce and Pavlowsky, 2014).
4.2. Vertical trace metal trends
The vertical trends in trace metals, percent organic matter, and
percent silt and clay for the eight sample cores that have AMS14C radio-
carbon ages are shown inFig. 3(A–H); vertical trends in trace metals,
percent organic matter, and percent silt and clay for theﬁve sites that
lack 14C ages are similar to those depicted inFig. 3. At the sites depicted,
14C ages in the lower half of the cores provide chronological control on
stratigraphy (seeKasielke and Zepp, 2011). The AMS dates, which were
obtained on charcoal fragments, are provided inTable 3.Ac o m p a r i s o n
of the percent silt and clay vertical trends with the trace metal vertical
trends (Horowitz, 1985) reveals no relationship between sediment
grain size and trace metal concentrations, similar to what I found in
previous work along the Lahn River (Martin, 2004). Likewise, organic
matter content has minimal effect on trace element concentrations in
the cores.
Generally, vertical trace metal peaks at individual core sites are
found at similar depths, suggesting that post-depositional movement
of metals has been minimal (Lecce and Pavlowsky, 2014). In a few
cores, the peak concentrations for the metals occur at slightly different
depths, usually within 0.10 m of one another. The different depths for
peak concentrations may result from metals having various upstream
sources that were active during different time periods, or result from
post-depositional, down-core movement of metals. In those cores
where the depth to peak concentrations differ, the metal trends are sim-
ilar, an indication that any post-depositional migration of metals has
been limited. The similarity in the depths to metals in individual cores
and similar metal trends suggest that the physical deposition of metals
by overbankﬂow rather than post-depositional migration of them ac-
counts for metal trends, and they can thus be used as stratigraphic
markers in cores. Typically cores extend to a depth of 0.90 to 1.0 m,
but in some instances the presence of sandy or gravelly layers prevented
deeper coring.
Vertical trends in trace metals are similar among cores, with a pro-
nounced peak in concentrations at a speciﬁc depth below theﬂoodplain
surface. Often, the increase in metal concentrations to the peak occurs
over a very short up-core distance (Fig. 3F). The maximum concentra-
tions for Cu, Pb, and Zn are typically at depths ranging from 0.20 to
0.70 m. The mean depths of the peak concentrations of Cu, Pb, and Zn
are 0.42, 0.38, and 0.36 m, respectively. For some metals in the three up-
stream cores (Fig. 3A, B, C), peak concentrations occur at two depths. For
example inFig. 3A, Zn concentrations peak at depths of 0.3 and 0.6 m.
The presence of a double peak, especially evident inFig. 3A for Zn and
in Fig. 3B for Cu and Zn, suggests an upstream source that was present
at a later date for those two trace metals.

in Fig. 3B for Cu and Zn, suggests an upstream source that was present
at a later date for those two trace metals. Detailed information on
mining operations and industrial activity in the Dill River valley is unfor-
tunately not available, so the secondary peaks in Cu and Zn cannot be
linked to a particular source or sources of trace metals. It is possible
that the secondary peaks are the result of remobilization by erosion of
metal-rich sediments from upstream, near-channel locations and con-
veyance of them downstream. If that is the case, metal-rich sediments
were deposited recently at the most upstream reaches of the study
area because those sites are closest to the source or sources. Down-
stream sites lack the more recent secondary peaks because insufﬁcient
time has elapsed for those metal-contaminated sediments to be
transported downstream. Interestingly, the secondary peak in Cu is
present only inFig. 3B. It may result from a recent local source of Cu
immediately upstream from the site. In contrast, a pronounced double
peak in Zn occurs inFig. 3Aa n d3B, suggesting a more extensive
upstream source (e.g., mine, industrial facility, or metals stored in
near-channel sediments) for Zn.
Radiocarbon ages on charcoal range from 1670 ± 30 RCYBP (Beta-
365179) to 90 ± 40 RCYBP (Beta-285118), indicating a late Holocene
age forﬂoodplain sediments. With the exception of cores D5 and D11
(Fig. 3Da n d3F), the dated charcoal was recovered below the peak con-
centrations; at the aforementioned cores, the charcoal was recovered at
nearly the same depth as peak trace metal concentrations. Radiocarbon
ages generally fall within the time period mid/late-1700s to around
1900 and provide a maximum age for overlying sediments. Assuming
that the maximum trace metal concentrations correspond to the period
of peak iron ore mining and steel mill operations upstream (mid-1800s
to mid-1900s), the AMS ages provide independent veriﬁcation that
deposition of metal-contaminated sediments commenced after the
mid/late seventeenth century. Sediments deposited most recently
(generally at depths above 0.20 m) are less contaminated with trace
metals, an indication that cleaner sediments have begun to move
through the watershed during the last several decades. A similar trend
has been noted in other studies in western Europe that examined

In a downstream direction, the depth of Cu, Pb, and Zn peak concen-
trations varies from site to site. As an example, at core D2 (Fig. 3A), an up-
stream site, peak concentrations of Cu, Pb, and Zn occur at depths of 0.5,
0.4, and 0.3 m, respectively; in contrast, at core D8 (Fig. 3B), which was
collected 7.5 km farther downstream, the peak concentrations of Cu, Pb,
and Zn are present at 0.7, 0.6, and 0.6 m, respectively. The most down-
stream sample (core D7 at 25 km downstream;Fig. 3H) contains maxi-
mum concentrations of all three trace elements at 0.2 m. The absence of
a systematic downstream trend in the depth to maximum trace metal
concentrations may be linked to geomorphic variables such asﬂoodplain
elevation above the active river channel (Lecce and Pavlowsky, 2014).
Multiple point sources of trace metals downstream (e.g., industrial facili-
ties) may also affect the depth at which maximum metal concentrations
are found by supplying high loads of contaminants to the river, thereby
masking the contribution of upstream metal sources. This may explain
the shallow depth at which peak concentrations are found in core D7
(Fig. 3H), which is located just downstream from several industrial facili-
ties. The different depths to peak concentrations within individual cores,
as noted previously, may result from metals having various upstream
sources that were active during different time periods or be the product
of some post-depositional, down-core movement of metals.
4.3. Recentﬂoodplain sedimentation
Radiocarbon ages from 8 of the 13 sediment cores allow estimation
of the amount of recentﬂoodplain sedimentation in the study reach.
Estimates of late Holoceneﬂoodplain sedimentation from this study
and from drainage basins in the vicinity of the Dill River are summarized
in Table 4. The radiocarbon ages from the Dill Riverﬂoodplain indicate
0.6 to 1 m of sedimentation over the last 150–300 years, or a sedimen-
tation rate of 0.2–0.3 cm y−1; the amount and rate of deposition are
greater than those found in other watersheds in the vicinity of
the study reach. Core D7 (Fig. 3H), the most downstream sample
location, had the greatest sedimentation of 0.8 to 1 m over about a
century (0.8 cm y−1); in contrast, at core AS1 (Fig. 3G), which is 1 km
upstream of site D7, 1.1 m of sedimentation over 300 years occurred
(0.4 cm y−1). The other sites with radiocarbon control suggest between
0.6 and 0.8 m of sedimentation over 150 to 200 years (0.3–0.4 cm y−1).
No downstream trend in the sedimentation amount was apparent;
some downstream sites (D7;Fig. 3H) had high sedimentation, whereas
others (AS1;Fig. 3G) had much less.
4.4. Trace metal storage in the Dill and Lahn river valleys
The mean trace metal concentrations noted here along the Dill River
exceed the values that I found at near-channel positions along the Lahn
River (Martin, 2004, 2012). Mean trace metal concentrations from 28
near-channel sites in the Marburg to Wetzlar reach of the Lahn River,
which is upstream of the Lahn River conﬂuence with the Dill River at
Wetzlar, are summarized inTable 5as are mean trace metal concentra-
tions at depths of 0–0.05 m along the Dill River. As the data reveal, mean
concentrations along the Dill River are higher than mean concentrations
along the Lahn River.

sediments along the Dill River contain higher concentrations of Cu, Pb,
and Zn than do sediments in a similar geomorphic position along the
Lahn River upstream of the conﬂuence of the Lahn and Dill Rivers at
Wetzlar. The source of these additional trace metals is likely anthropo-
genic activity in the form of mining, industrial activity, or both.
5. Discussion
Core samples collected at 13 near-channel sites along theﬂoodplain
of the Dill River reveal concentrations of Cu, Pb, and Zn that exceed
background concentrations, with the highest level of trace metals in
the upper 0.40 m of cores. Mean concentrations of Cu, Pb, and Zn exceed
the ‘precautionary value’ contained in the German Federal Soil Protec-
tion Act (Bundes-Bodenschutzgesetz {BbodSchG}); some individual
samples have concentrations of Cu, Pb, and Zn that are several times
the ‘precautionary value’. Nearly all samples in the upper 0.4 m contain
concentrations of Cu, Pb, and Zn that exceed the‘precautionary value’ of
the German standards and the TEC (threshold effect contamination) of
McDonald et al. (2000). The peak concentration of all three trace metals
tend to be found at depths of 0.20 to 0.70 m, with lower concentrations
up-core toward the surface. This trend suggests that the release of the
trace metals to the environment has decreased over the last several de-
cades, aﬁnding noted in other studies from western Europe of metal
contamination levels inﬂoodplain sediments (e.g.,Brügmann, 1995;
Scherer et al., 2003; Martin, 2012; Zachmann et al., 2013; Vallius, 2014).
Mean and maximum trace metal concentration do not systemat-
ically decrease with distance downstream (Fig. 2), suggesting multi-
ple nonpoint sources rather than a single point source for trace metal
contamination in the watershed ( Lecce and Pavlowsky, 2014 ).
Although the upper Dill River basin has a history of iron ore mining,
with the peak period of mining activity between 1870 and 1945,
there are other possible sources for trace metals in the catchment, in-
cluding but not limited to industrial activity in upstream urban areas
such as Dillenburg and Herborn. A variety of sources for the trace
metals likely account for the absence of a downstream distance
decay in metal contamination. Given multiple sources for metals
along the river, a decrease in metal concentrations with distance
downstream would be unexpected as additional metals have been
introduced to the study reach at various locations. The absence of a
distance decay downstream could also reﬂect the episodic move-
ment of metals downstream through the study reach. Although
reductions in the release of trace metals to watersheds have been
linked to reduced contamination in downstream ﬂoodplain sedi-
ments (Ciszewski, 2003; Grosbois etal., 2006; Bábek et al., 2008),
several decades may pass before declines in metal releases are
reﬂected in downstream sediments (Outridge et al., 2011). If that is
the case, near-channel sediments along the Dill River may serve as
potential sources of downstream trace metal pollution in the fore-
seeable future, something noted by others working in western
European watersheds (e.g., Förstner, 2003; Krüger et al., 2005;
Macklin et al., 2006; Foulds et al., 2014; Resongles et al., 2014).
General knowledge of the upstream mining history in the Dill
River and AMS radiocarbon ages on charcoal from the sediment
cores provide chronologic control on recentﬂoodplain sedimenta-
tion in the study reach. The vertical trends in trace metal concen-
trations display a pronounced peak at speciﬁc depths below the
ﬂoodplain surface, generally between 0.20 and 0.70 m (Fig. 3,A –
H). The peak is presumed to correspond with the period of maxi-
mum metal releases to the environment through mining and
industrial activities (e.g., steel mill operations) upstream in the
watershed.

__data__.text:
General knowledge of the upstream mining history in the Dill
River and AMS radiocarbon ages on charcoal from the sediment
cores provide chronologic control on recentﬂoodplain sedimenta-
tion in the study reach. The vertical trends in trace metal concen-
trations display a pronounced peak at speciﬁc depths below the
ﬂoodplain surface, generally between 0.20 and 0.70 m (Fig. 3,A –
H). The peak is presumed to correspond with the period of maxi-
mum metal releases to the environment through mining and
industrial activities (e.g., steel mill operations) upstream in the
watershed. Similarities among vertical treads in cores indicate
that post-depositional movement of metals has been minimal.
The radiocarbon ages, which come from depths at or below the
peak metal concentrations, provide maximum ages for sediments
at depths of 0.60 to 1.10 m. The radiocarbon ages indicate that de-
position of metal-contaminated sediments commenced after the
mid/late seventeenth century, which corresponds well with the
history of metal releases to the environment. With the exception
of core D7 (Fig. 3H), the other radiocarbon-dated cores place the
peak metal concentration at 100 to 150 years ago, or during the
late 1800s and early 1900s. Cores D2, D11, AS2, and D5 (Fig. 3A,
D, E, F), which range from the upstream reach of the study area to
the most downstream reach, all suggest the deposition of peak
metal-contaminated sediments in the late 1800s to early 1900s.
The sample site whose vertical metal trends and radiocarbon ages
are an anomaly is core D7 (Fig. 3H). Here, the radiocarbon ages
are very young, and the peak metal concentrations occur at an un-
usually shallow depth of 0.15–0.20 m. As the most downstream
sample site, the location may have received additions of trace
metals eroded from upstream sites since the mid-1900s.
Aside from site D7, where radiocarbon ages indicate about 1.0 m of
sediment deposition during the 1900s, radiocarbon ages and trace
metal trends from the other cores in the study reach document 0.6 to
1.1 m ofﬂoodplain sedimentation over the last 150 to 300 years (0.2–
0.3 cm y−1). This amount exceeds recentﬂoodplain sedimentation
documented in nearby watersheds (Lang and Nolte, 1999; Rittweger,
2000; Kalis et al., 2003; Houben, 2012). Work elsewhere in Germany
has noted rapid increases inﬂoodplain sedimentation beginning about
1000 years ago. Increased sedimentation has been ascribed to expanded
agricultural activity, wetter climate conditions, or a combination thereof
(Fuchs et al., 2011; Raab et al., 2011). There is little evidence in the liter-
ature of high rates of sedimentation such as those documented here
along the Dill River having occurred over the last 300 years. The rela-
tively rugged terrain of the Dill River basin may have resulted in high
sediment delivery to the valley over the last several hundred years,
especially during periods when the forest cover was reduced by expan-
sion of agriculture and perhaps mining activity. The uncertainty
involved with radiocarbon ages notwithstanding, the calculated sedi-
mentation rates in the study reach range from 0.06 cm to 1.2 cm y−1,
with a mean calculated sedimentation rate for the dated cores
(n = 10) of 0.56 cm y−1 (standard deviation = 0.3 cm y−1), a rate
higher than has been noted in surrounding watersheds.
Initially, I began work in the Dill River basin after noting that trace
metal storage along the Lahn River was greater downstream from
Wetzlar, which marks the conﬂuence of the Lahn and Dill Rivers
(Martin, 2004, 2012). Results here from the core samples along the
Dill River indicate that the concentration of trace metals inﬂoodplain
sediments is higher in the Dill River valley than in the Lahn River valley
(Table 5).
